newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CDU subdued ahead of Kohl's new record.
newsitem.headline: German CDU subdued ahead of Kohl's new record.

text.p: Helmut Kohl's political morning after is dawning even before the tireless chancellor has been out on the town to celebrate the record he sets next week as post-war Germany's longest-serving leader.
A sudden storm over taxes and budgets dampened the mood just before the annual congress of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) was held on Monday and Tuesday in Hanover.
Scattered rumblings inside the convention hall, which Kohl's lieutenants otherwise kept as a debate-free zone, foreshadowed even more thunder clouds looming over the horizon.

Hemmed in by globalisation, the Maastricht criteria and an ageing population, Germany is heading for a crunch that will severely test the famed consensus style that helped the country rise like a phoenix from the ashes of World War Two.
To keep its competitive edge, this smugly comfortable society must scale down its welfare state, shed budget fat, cut the high costs for labour and close tax loopholes for the rich.
Kohl, a great practitioner of consensus politics, gave his party a gloomy forecast for the coming months.

"Most people in this country have long realised that we can't go on like this," he warned, sounding more like an opposition leader than the wily chancellor who has led and shaped the country for the past 14 years. "It's a few minutes before 12 o'clock and we have to make decisions now."
His closest allies, CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble and Finance Minister Theo Waigel, were just as glum.
"Whoever wants to push through reforms in Germany that do not only redistribute goodies has to have courage and stamina," Schaeuble said to stiffen resolve in the rank and file.
"These are dammed tough times," a grim-faced Waigel said.

Kohl has already had trouble introducing some of the reforms he wants to see over the next two years to be ready for Germany's next general election in late 1998 and the start of Europe's single currency at the start of the following year.

Opposition Social Democrats (SPD), trade unions and even some members of his own centre-right coalition opposed decisions this year to extend shop-closing hours, cut back sick pay benefits and make hiring and firing easier for small firms.

The going got rougher last week when Waigel, searching for a few billion more marks to finance his 1997 budget without overstepping Maastricht deficit limits, forced Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners to put off a promised tax cut that they had been touting as their biggest victory in years.

The deep split that feud caused was a bad omen for the radical tax reform the CDU agreed to at its Hanover congress. Under the plan, peak rates will fall from 53 to 35 percent while starting rates will slide from 25.9 to under 20 percent.

Waigel welcomed the reform but promptly warned he will need allies to battle entrenched vested interests, close tax loopholes and rake in the extra revenues needed to offset the 30 billion marks ($19.58 billion) that will be given back to the taxpayers.
"There can't be two different roles in the coalition, with one side doing the dirty work in the quarry while the other side sells the marble," he said.

Although delegates backed the tax plan with only one dissenting vote, the short flash of debate on narrowing a single loophole -- a tax credit for commuters driving their own cars to work -- hinted at how much resistance lurked out there.
Kohl did not even allow any debate on reforming the generous pension system, which is growing increasingly shaky as ever fewer young Germans pay for ever more elderly people.
Critics who suggest this means the retired are robbing the young had no chance to air their views as party leaders left no time for discussion after Labour Minister Norbert Bluem spoke.
While warning the delegates about the tough decisions to come, Kohl cautiously backed off from an earlier pledge to help create two million more jobs by the year 2000.
"I would be satisfied if we could reach two-thirds of that number," he said, almost in passing, during his opening speech. $1=1.5323 Mark)
